title: Tug of war on a spring scale
hook: Two friends pull a rope from opposite ends. What does a scale in the middle read?

knows: a pull is a force in newtons
a spring scale measures a pull
doesNotKnow: that a scale reads the tension passed through it, so two equal opposite 100 N pulls give 100 N
that a wall pulls back exactly as hard as a second person would

misconception: Two people each pulling 100 N on a rope make the scale in the middle read 200 N (or 0 N, because the pulls cancel).
objective: The learner can explain that a scale pulled from both ends reads the tension passed through it: 100 N when each end is pulled with 100 N, whether by a friend or a wall.

claims.text: A massless spring scale at rest has equal pulls on its two ends and reads that one common tension (stage: two equal 'tension' arrows on the spring, dial; reveal: 'But a scale at rest reads the one pull passing through it: the tension its two ends share.').
claims.source: v3 2026-10-16 (learner r11 finding 3): reveal sentence 'at rest it is stretched only when both ends are pulled equally' replaced (it read as 'equal pulls are what stretch it'); the claim's physics is unchanged; reset to unverified. | Newton's second law with a = 0 and m ~ 0: T_right - T_left = m a = 0, so both ends carry the same tension, which the spring carries once (artifacts/scratch/cm-physics-r4/check.mjs, block 'tug-of-war-scale'). Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, chapter on Newton's laws (tension). Brief claim 1. | prior note: FC pass 66 (fact-checker, 2026-10-16, SO-10-2 [project:wave-j], server 987687a, walkthrough 2026-10-16T14:42Z via --url http://localhost:3591): VERIFIED. Own derivation: for the scale, T_right - T_left = m a; at rest (a = 0) the two end pulls are equal for any mass, and a massless spring in series carries that one tension, which the dial reads. Code: Demo.tsx draws both arrows and the dial from one value T = PULL[mode] (100, 100, 200 N). Opened OpenStax University Physics (CC BY 4.0) CNXML from raw.githubusercontent.com/openstax/osbooks-university-physics-bundle at 2300d5b (fetched 2026-10-16 by this pass): vol 1 m58303 'Solving Problems with Newton's Laws': 'Since the string and the pulley have negligible mass ... the tension is the same throughout the string'; vol 1 m58300 'Common Forces': 'tension force pulls outward along the two ends of a rope'. Stage seen on the server (step 1): two equal orange arrows on the spring, 'tension 100 N', dial 100 N. Reveal seen: 'at rest it is stretched only when both ends are pulled equally', which is exact (the 2026-10-14 wording note is resolved). Wording adopted by the builder (0f8fa45, demo-builder) per W-711; r2 ruling on W-1108. Previous record (v1): status verified, fact-checker 2026-10-14: Derivation (Halliday et al. not opened): for a massless scale T_right - T_left = m a = 0, and a spring in series carries that one tension. Wording note for demo-builder (not blocking): the reveal's 'it can only be stretched if both ends are pulled equally' is true for the idealised massless scale at rest (c4), but not for a real scale that is accelerating. 'At rest, it is stretched only when both ends are pulled equally' would be exact.

claims.text: A wall holding the rope's end pulls back with the same 100 N as the friend pulls (stage: wall with a 100 N arrow; reveal: 'the wall pulls back exactly as hard, just as the second friend did').
claims.source: Newton's third law: the rope pulls the wall 100 N, the wall pulls the rope 100 N. artifacts/scratch/cm-physics-r4/check.mjs; Halliday, Resnick and Walker, same chapter. Brief claim 2.
claims.note: Derivation: Newton's third law. The rope pulls the wall 100 N and the wall pulls the rope 100 N; the stage draws the right-hand arrow as 100 N.

claims.text: Each friend pulling 100 N gives a reading of 100 N; one friend and a wall gives 100 N; each pulling 200 N gives 200 N (stage dial and Seen row '100 + 100: 100 N · wall: 100 N · 200 + 200: 200 N'; reveal quotes the three readings recorded at the milestones).
claims.source: artifacts/scratch/cm-physics-r4/check.mjs prints reads_N = 100, 100, 200 for the three cases. Demo.tsx PULL. Brief claim 3.
claims.note: Check script re-run (artifacts/scratch/cm-physics-r4/check.mjs, 'scale'): 100, 100, 200 N; Demo.tsx PULL matches; the Seen row and reveal quote PULL at each milestone.

claims.text: Idealisations: the rope and scale are massless and everything is at rest. The spring's stretch and the arrow lengths on the stage are drawn in proportion to the tension, not to scale.
claims.source: Stated assumption, brief claim 4. Demo.tsx: half-length 22 + 0.05 px per N; arrows 0.12 px per N. Not shown as a sentence on the stage; recorded here.
claims.note: Convention, checked against the code: half-length 22 + 0.05 px/N, arrows 0.12 px/N; massless, at rest.

claims.text: The two friends' pulls on the scale are equal and opposite, so the net force on it is zero and it stays still; the 0 N answer mistakes that zero net force for the reading, which is the tension, the one pull passing through it (reveal: 'not 200 or 0. The two pulls do cancel: that is why the scale stays still.').
claims.source: New in v3 (learner r11 finding 3, the 0 N picker). Newton's second law on the massless scale: T_right - T_left = m a = 0 (Demo.tsx header comment), so the end pulls cancel (net force zero, at rest) while each end carries the same tension T = 100 N, which the spring's stretch and the dial show. 'Not 0' and 'not 200' are the two wrong options of the predict card; the reading 100 N is c3.

recall.question: A 50 N weight hangs from each end of a string that runs over two pulleys, with a spring scale in the middle of the string. What does the scale read?
recall.why: The scale reads the tension passed through the string. Each weight pulls 50 N, so the tension is 50 N; the second weight plays the part a wall would.
